title: High Water Marks and Crystallisation
summary: The rule that stops a hedge fund charging you twice for the same gain — and the ways it gets weakened.

lesson.body:
A [[hedge-fund|hedge fund]] charges a [[carried-interest|performance fee]] on gains. That raises an obvious question: gains from where?

Without a rule, a fund could fall 20%, recover 20%, and charge a performance fee on the recovery — billing you for getting back to where you started. The rule that prevents this is the **[[high-water-mark]]**: the highest value your investment has previously reached. Performance fees are only charged on gains **above** that level.

The mechanism is per-investor, not per-fund, because different investors subscribe at different times. Your high water mark is your own.

**[[crystallisation]]** is the related term: how often the performance fee is actually calculated and taken. Annually is the common answer. It matters because between crystallisation dates, gains and losses offset — and after one, they no longer do.
You invest at 100. The fund's value per unit then goes 100 → 80 → 95 → 110.
walkthrough: **Falls to 80.** No performance fee — you are below your high water mark. The mark stays at 100.
**Recovers to 95.** Still no fee. You are up 18.75% from the trough and still below where you started, and the mark remains 100.
**Rises to 110.** Now a fee is charged, and only on the **10** above the high water mark. The mark then resets to 110.
**Total fee base across the whole path: 10.** Which matches your actual gain of 10. That is the high water mark working exactly as intended.
**Now suppose the mark had been reset to 80 after the fall.** Fees would be charged on 95 - 80 = 15, then on 110 - 95 = 15. **A fee base of 30 against an actual gain of 10 — three times over.**
Read that carefully. The reset is not a small adjustment. It triples what you pay on the same performance.

lesson.body:
The high water mark exists because of a genuine asymmetry: **the manager shares the upside and not the downside.**

A performance fee is a call option on the fund's gains, granted by the investor. Options are worth more when the underlying is volatile, so a manager holding one has a structural incentive toward risk that the investor does not share. The high water mark constrains that — it means a manager who loses money has to earn it back before being paid again, which restores some symmetry.

But notice what it does *not* do, because this is the part people miss. **A high water mark does not make the manager whole for your loss; it merely stops them profiting from the recovery.** If a fund falls 30% and takes three years to recover, you have lost three years and the manager has lost three years of performance fees. Nobody compensates you for the time.

And there is a harder problem. A manager deep below their high water mark has a difficult set of incentives: their performance fee is worthless unless the fund recovers substantially, so **taking more risk becomes rational for them and not for you.** Alternatively they close the fund and start a new one with a fresh mark — which is the same outcome as a reset, achieved differently.

**Fund closure and relaunch.** The most complete way around a high water mark. A manager well below their mark closes, returns capital, and launches a new vehicle with the same strategy and a fresh mark. Perfectly legal, and it eliminates the constraint entirely.

**Explicit reset provisions.** Some agreements permit a reset after a defined period below the mark, or a partial reset. Worth reading for, and rare in institutional terms.

**Modified or rolling high water marks.** Variations where the mark amortises over time or resets to a proportion of the shortfall. These are not always unreasonable — a permanent mark can trap a manager after an extreme loss — but they are a weakening and should be priced as one.

**Frequent crystallisation.** Quarterly rather than annual crystallisation means gains in one quarter are charged even if a later quarter reverses them. Over a volatile year with a flat outcome, an investor can pay meaningful fees. **Less frequent crystallisation is straightforwardly better for the investor.**

**Equalisation mechanics.** Where investors subscribe at different times, funds use series accounting or equalisation adjustments so each investor's own mark is respected. These are legitimate and complicated; the risk is a poorly implemented method that quietly charges new investors for gains earned before they arrived.

**Fees on unrealised gains.** If a fund holds illiquid positions marked by the manager, a performance fee crystallised annually is being paid on the manager's own valuations. That is a genuine conflict, and side-pocketing illiquid positions is the usual remedy.

lesson.body:
**Ask what happened to the manager's previous funds, not just how this one performed.** A manager with a strong three-year record on a fund launched shortly after closing a loss-making predecessor has, in economic substance, reset their high water mark — and the new record does not include the loss you would have suffered had you been there throughout.

This is not usually deceptive. Fund closures happen for many reasons and a relaunch can be entirely legitimate. But the track record you are being shown starts at a convenient point, and establishing whether an earlier vehicle exists is a factual question with a factual answer. **The relevant history is the manager's, not the fund's.**

**Ask how often the performance fee crystallises.** Annual is standard; quarterly is worse for you and worth quantifying at a plausible volatility.

**Ask whether the high water mark can reset, under any circumstance.** Then read the clause rather than accepting the answer, because "no" and "no, except after twenty-four months below" are both said quickly.

**Ask whether performance fees are charged on unrealised gains, and how illiquid positions are handled.** If the fund can hold hard-to-value assets and crystallises annually, the manager is being paid on its own marks.

**Ask whether there is a hurdle on the performance fee at all.** Many hedge funds have none, meaning a fee is charged on returns you could have earned in cash. In a high-rate environment that is a substantial giveaway.

**Ask about the manager's prior vehicles.** Specifically whether any were closed while below their high water mark.

**Ask how much of the manager's own money is in the fund, and whether it is subject to the same terms.** A manager invested alongside you on the same terms has skin in both directions.

items: A high water mark restricts performance fees to gains above your previous peak, so you are not charged twice for the same recovery.
In the worked path, a reset would have tripled the fee base — 30 against an actual gain of 10.
It stops the manager profiting from a recovery; it does not compensate you for the time lost, and it can push a manager far below the mark toward more risk.
Closing a fund and relaunching resets the mark completely. The relevant track record is the manager's, not the fund's.

questions.stem: You invest at 100. The fund goes to 80, then 95, then 110. With a permanent high water mark, what total gain is a performance fee charged on?
questions.explanation: No fee at 80 or 95 — both are below the mark of 100. At 110 the fee applies to the 10 above the mark. Total fee base of 10, matching your actual gain of 10, which is the mechanism working correctly.

questions.stem: Same path (100 → 80 → 95 → 110), but the high water mark resets to 80 after the fall. What total gain would fees be charged on?
questions.explanation: Fees on 95 - 80 = 15, then on 110 - 95 = 15, totalling 30 — against an actual gain of 10. Three times the fee base for the same performance, which is why a reset provision is not a technicality.

questions.stem: Why is quarterly crystallisation worse for the investor than annual?
choices: Because quarterly fees are charged at a higher rate
Because gains in one quarter are charged even if a later quarter reverses them, so a flat year can still cost fees
Because quarterly crystallisation eliminates the high water mark
Because it prevents the manager from taking risk
rationales: The rate is the same. It is the frequency of the calculation that changes the outcome.
Correct. Within a crystallisation period gains and losses offset. Crystallise four times a year and a volatile but ultimately flat year can generate real fees on gains that did not survive.
The high water mark still applies. More frequent crystallisation weakens its practical effect without removing it.
Crystallisation frequency does not constrain risk-taking, and if anything more frequent payment reduces the manager's exposure to subsequent losses.
questions.explanation: The general rule: longer crystallisation periods mean more offsetting, which favours the investor. It is a term that sounds administrative and is straightforwardly economic — the same pattern as the fee base.

questions.stem: "A high water mark means the manager shares our downside." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — it stops the manager profiting from the recovery, but they lose only future fees, never their own capital
False — high water marks do not affect manager compensation at all
True — the manager cannot be paid until losses are recovered, which is sharing the downside
False — because managers are compensated for losses through the management fee
rationales: Correct. You lose capital; the manager forgoes fees they had not yet earned. Both are real and they are not the same thing — and nobody compensates you for the time spent recovering.
They very much do — that is their entire function.
Forgoing future income is a genuine cost and it is not sharing a loss. The asymmetry remains: your capital falls, their income pauses.
The management fee continues regardless, which strengthens rather than weakens the point about asymmetry.
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because it identifies what actually aligns a manager with your downside: their own capital invested on the same terms. The high water mark limits the upside they can extract; only [[co-investment|co-investment]] gives them a loss.

questions.stem: A manager shows a strong three-year record on a fund launched shortly after closing a previous, loss-making vehicle with the same strategy. What have they effectively done?
choices: Demonstrated that they learned from the earlier fund
Reset their high water mark, so the record shown excludes the loss an investor present throughout would have suffered
Breached their fiduciary duty to the prior fund's investors
Nothing significant, since fund closures are common
rationales: They may well have. That is a separate and unverifiable claim, and it does not change what the track record omits.
Correct. A new vehicle starts with a fresh mark, so performance fees accrue from the new baseline. The three-year record is accurate and starts at a convenient point.
Closing a fund is generally permitted and often appropriate. Nothing here implies a breach, which is why framing it as a structural observation rather than an accusation is the right approach.
Closures are common and this specific sequence — closing below the mark, relaunching the same strategy — is exactly the case where it matters.
questions.explanation: The useful reframing is that you are underwriting a manager, not a fund. Asking for the full history of vehicles run, including closed ones, is a factual request — and the answer is informative whichever way it goes.

questions.stem: A hedge fund charges 20% performance fees with a high water mark but no hurdle, when cash yields 5%. Why is that worth challenging?
choices: Because high water marks are ineffective without a hurdle
Because a fee is charged on the first 5% of return, which was available risk-free
Because performance fees are prohibited without a hurdle
Because 20% is above the market standard rate
rationales: The high water mark functions perfectly well without a hurdle. They address different problems.
Correct. With no hurdle, the manager earns 20% of a return you could have had in a deposit account. In a high-rate environment that is a meaningful transfer for no skill.
There is no such prohibition. Many hedge funds have no hurdle, which is exactly why it is worth raising.
20% is broadly standard. The rate is not the issue; the absence of a threshold is.
questions.explanation: This became a much larger issue as rates rose. A fee on the cash return is pure giveaway, and asking for a cash hurdle is a specific, reasonable request that some managers will accept and others will not — which is itself informative.
